analysis.brief_en: A scientific review published on November 18, 2026, in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology links the immune evasion mechanisms of the SFTS virus to clinical treatment challenges. The virus, classified as Dabie bandavirus, is a tick-borne pathogen first identified in Henan Province in 2009. National surveillance in China from 2010 to 2023 documented 27,447 confirmed cases with an overall case fatality rate of 4.83 percent, which has decreased over time. However, hospital cohorts of severely ill patients report fatality rates between 12 percent and 30 percent, with intensive care mortality reaching 50 percent. The review highlights the virus's ability to disrupt host immune pathways, including the type I interferon pathway and adaptive immunity, leading to severe disease outcomes. The virus is designated a priority pathogen by the World Health Organization since 2017, and its potential for international spread is underscored by the detection of its primary vector, the Asian longhorned tick, in the United States. The study also notes that human-to-human transmission occurs through direct blood or fluid contact, as evidenced by a 2023 outbreak in Zhejiang Province where seven of twelve cases were linked to such exposure. The findings emphasize the need for improved clinical translation and the exploration of novel immunomodulatory treatments, such as Janus kinase inhibitors and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, to address the virus's complex immune evasion strategies.

title: Machine Learning Model Predicts In-Hospital Mortality in Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: The study was published on November 14, 2026. The internal validation cohort was evaluated on the same date, with the model's performance metrics reported as of that date.
analysis.location_and_population: The study involved clinical data from 238 patients diagnosed with severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, including 177 survivors and 61 non-survivors. The cohort was split into a training group of 167 patients and a validation group of 71 patients.
analysis.event: A machine learning model was developed to predict in-hospital mortality in patients with severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, based on viral, immune, and inflammatory biomarkers. The model was validated internally and demonstrated an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.841.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The model's internal validation showed a sensitivity of 0.944 and specificity of 0.698, with a Brier score of 0.139. The syndrome is characterized by an excessive inflammatory response and impaired adaptive immunity, which carry a substantial risk of mortality.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study emphasized that while the model showed favorable internal validation metrics, rigorous multicenter prospective evaluation is necessary before recommending it for routine clinical use. The model was translated into a graphical nomogram and an interactive web-based risk calculator for practical implementation.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on November 14, 2026, by Bioengineer.org introduced a machine learning model that predicts in-hospital mortality in patients with severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS). The model integrates viral, immune, and inflammatory biomarkers, including SFTSV RNA load, CD3+CD4+ T-cell count, interleukin-6, and procalcitonin. It was validated using an internal cohort of 71 patients, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.841. The model demonstrated high sensitivity (0.944) and moderate specificity (0.698), with a Brier score of 0.139. Researchers highlighted the need for multicenter prospective evaluation before clinical adoption. The model was developed using Boruta feature selection, LASSO, and random forest recursive feature elimination, and was made interpretable through SHAP methods. It was translated into a graphical nomogram and a web-based risk calculator for point-of-care use.

title: Scoping Review Identifies Broad Animal Hosts Driving Severe Fever With Thrombocytopenia Virus

analysis.time: The scoping review was conducted from January 1, 2011, through October 21, 2025, with the publication date on November 17, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on East Asia, including China, Japan, and the Republic of Korea, with specific mention of a mink farm in Weihai, China, and endemic rural agricultural zones.
analysis.event: A scoping review identified the broad animal hosts involved in the maintenance and transmission of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV), including domestic livestock, peri-domestic mammals, free-roaming wildlife, and household companion animals. The review also documented an outbreak on a mink farm in Weihai, China, where two human cases were linked to the virus.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The virus circulates across at least 15 animal species, with domestic livestock showing high seroprevalence rates. Case-fatality ratios range between 5% and 30%, with higher mortality in older adults and those with comorbid conditions. The outbreak on the mink farm showed potential transmission via aerosols or direct contact with blood and tissues.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The review highlights the need for public health messaging that addresses multiple transmission interfaces, including those involving domestic, agricultural, and clinical environments. The study was conducted under an integrated One Health framework and included systematic literature searches and meta-analyses.

analysis.brief_en: A scoping review of 353 studies has identified the broad range of vertebrate hosts that contribute to the maintenance and transmission of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV), including domestic livestock, peri-domestic mammals, free-roaming wildlife, and household companion animals. The review, published on November 17, 2026, highlights that SFTSV is an emerging tick-borne zoonosis, primarily transmitted by Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks, with additional vector species also implicated. The study found that domestic livestock, such as sheep, goats, and cattle, show high seroprevalence rates, and an outbreak on a mink farm in Weihai, China, linked two human cases to the virus, suggesting potential transmission via aerosols or direct contact with infected animals. Case-fatality ratios range from 5% to 30%, with higher mortality observed in older adults and those with comorbid conditions. The review emphasizes the need for comprehensive public health strategies that address multiple transmission routes, including those involving livestock handlers and pet owners, as current messaging often focuses solely on tick bites.

analysis.time: In recent years, the number of patients with SFTS has been increasing in Japan. In 2025, 191 patients were reported nationwide, marking a record high (provisional value).
analysis.location_and_population: Japan, with cases mainly concentrated in western Japan previously, but now infections are being confirmed in eastern Japan as well.
analysis.event: SFTS is an infectious disease caused by the tick, mainly transmitted through bites from infected ticks. It can be fatal if it becomes severe, with a case fatality rate of approximately 10–30% for patients in Japan. Dogs and cats can also be infected with SFTS, and there is direct transmission from infected animals to humans.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In 2024, 194 cats and 12 dogs were reported to have developed the disease in Japan. SFTS is a zoonotic disease and is classified as a Category IV infectious disease under Japan's Infectious Diseases Control Law. It can be transmitted to humans through contact with the blood, saliva, etc., of infected cats and dogs.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Infection control measures are extremely important when examining animals suspected of having SFTS. Veterinary professionals should use gloves, masks, gowns, eye protection, avoid direct contact with blood, saliva, excrement, be careful of bites and scratches, properly clean and disinfect instruments, and implement isolation and traffic line management for suspected cases. Favipiravir was approved in Japan in 2024 as a treatment for humans, but it has not been established as a standard treatment for dogs and cats.

SFTS, caused by the tick, is primarily transmitted through bites but can also be spread from infected dogs and cats to humans. The disease has been increasingly reported in both western and eastern Japan, raising concerns about its spread. SFTS can be fatal, with a case fatality rate of approximately 10–30% in Japan. In 2024, 194 cats and 12 dogs were reported to have developed the disease. Veterinary professionals are advised to implement strict infection control measures, including the use of protective gear and avoiding direct contact with infected animals. While favipiravir is approved for human treatment, it is not yet established as a standard treatment for dogs and cats. The report emphasizes the importance of vigilance and proper handling of suspected cases to prevent transmission.
